utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Is the reason why the witness is not in the matter raised by Mr. Robinson yesterday? Probably, yes. Regarding that matter, Mr. Robinson, we are concerned that given Mr. Karadzic's status as a self-represented accused, that this is not the usual situation where lead counsel takes responsibility for the entire Defence team, including any interns who might be permitted to be in the courtroom. I wonder whether you have anything to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll be happy to take responsibility for them, Mr. President. Even though I'm not lead counsel, I'm subject to the code of conduct, and I think I would be responsible for them in any event under the Registry's regime. So they've held that the code of conduct applies to those of us working as legal advisors for a self-represented accused. So I think I'll be happy to take responsibility for our interns. They're a very integral part of our team. We rely on them because of the resource issues that we have and because they're extremely talented. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One further clarification is whether your request is limited to the remainder of Ambassador Okun's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I intended it to apply to the remainder of the trial, actually. Which -- we have one intern who is assigned to each witness. They prepare summaries of the witness's prior testimony and prior statements for Dr. Karadzic, including the references to the transcripts, and then secondly they're tasked with preparing a summary of the witness's in-court testimony and the 92 ter materials. So I would like to bring in one intern who is assigned to that particular witness to both assist Dr. Karadzic if necessary and also help them to prepare the work that they have to do after the witness leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one further final clarification is this: As you confirmed yesterday, in our order it is stated that Mr. Karadzic would be permitted to have two members of his Defence team in the courtroom at any given time unless otherwise authorised by the Chamber. We take it that you are requesting such exceptional authorisation rather than suggesting that your intern would replace either yourself or Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will muse on the matter further and give you a ruling after the first break. Unless there's anything, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, have you come to a decision concerning whether the cross-examination would commence today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no clue when the examination-in-chief could be concluded. We'll see. Mr. Tieger, how much longer do you expect today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The estimate was three hours. I'm not sure -- quite sure how much I did before. I expected, although it's always a bit difficult, to come in roughly around that time. So my best estimate at this point is that I would conclude at the end of the session or some point into the next session. As I said, that's my best estimate at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, we'll see how it goes on, and we'll give our ruling later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, we'll be referring again to your note-books or diaries if you want to begin. They may already be in the order you wish, but I wanted to alert you to that so you could have them available for the easiest access. Ambassador, yesterday you testified concerning the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina sought by the accused and the Bosnian Serb leadership, the demographics of those areas, including the number of Muslims who lived there and some of the positions that the accused had about Muslims. I wanted to ask you, then, directly, whether the accused told you whether the ethnicities in Bosnia could live together or should be segregated, separated.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic said more than once that the ethnic groups could not live together and had to be separated. He added that perhaps one day, undetermined, in the future that might happen but that at present they could not live together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, you referred to more than one meeting at which you indicated such references were made, including the meeting of March 6, 1993, and April 24th, 1993. I wanted to turn your attention to a couple of additional meetings referenced in the journals. The first is found at the 17th of September, 1992. That's P00785, at page 25. And for you, Ambassador, that would be ICFY book number 2, the meeting that began at 9.10. And the particular reference should be found at page 5 of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Ambassador. I'm waiting for the version to come up on screen for the benefit of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There may be a mistake in the reference I gave, Your Honour. That was formerly 65 ter number 06535, which I understood had now become P00785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's correct. Diary number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the e-court page should be page 25, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, if I could direct your attention to the entry on the page to the right now showing on the screen in the middle of the page, can you read what that says and indicate to the Court whether or not that's another reference to the fact that the -- that Dr. Karadzic's position was that the nations, the ethnicities, in Bosnia, could not live together?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is another reference. Dr. Karadzic said: "The communities," meaning the ethnic communities, "cannot live together at present, too much hate. "We need the towns, the individual towns, to run themselves." Then Lord Owen asked him: "Could you imagine yourself with Muslims?" And Dr. Karadzic replied: "Over time we'll either get closer or more distant. "Some issues could still be in common, energy/water supply," that sort of thing. We asked about the judiciary, and he said: "No, not with Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could next turn your attention to the meeting of the 19th of September, 1992. Again that's P00785, this time at page 44, and that would be a meeting at 5.00, Mr. Ambassador, on the second page of the meeting. And this appears to be a meeting with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha, and Mr. Misa Milosevic, and on the page to the right, toward the bottom of the page, there's a comment by Dr. Koljevic. And if you could read that and indicate again whether that reflects the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership that the ethnicities could not live together.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nikola Koljevic, who is the last person speaking on that page, initials KOL, said that: "The war has shattered trust. The communities cannot live together any more. To deny that is fantasy." He continued by saying that: "Only by having borders can we begin to do away with borders." And I then summed up the presentation by saying: "Lengthy expatiation by Koljevic and Dr. Karadzic on that point." Nikola Koljevic was a -- now dead, was an eminent Shakespearian scholar with flawless English, and he liked to use his English, which is no surprise, so that's how you get a statement that "Only by having borders can we begin to do away with borders." We saw a good deal of him along with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, yesterday we had an opportunity to look at a still from the video that was of Mr. Krajisnik at the ethnic map with the overlay, and as reflected in the testimony in Krajisnik, during the course of speaking about that map, Mr. Krajisnik said that the territories shown within the horseshoe area belonged to the Serbs and that they were not holding territories ethnically populated by other national communities. And that could be found at page 4303 of the transcript. Ambassador, by that time, that is, in the latter part of 1992, was it correct that the other national communities were no longer populating those areas shown within the horseshoe area controlled by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was largely true due to the ethnic cleansing of those areas, particularly the western bank of the Drina River, where I mentioned yesterday there had been seven majority Muslim opstinas, and they were all occupied and taken by the Bosnian Serbs and the Yugoslav Army. And then in the Posavina area, around Brcko, which was a very important target for the Bosnian Serbs, and in the west region, west of Banja Luka, around Prijedor, was another area. But the two main areas for the cleansing were the Drina River and the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can you tell the Court from what sources you and Secretary Vance, Lord Owen, and others received information about the ethnic cleansing to which you referred?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in regular touch, that is to say, steady contact, with the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had delegates all over the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Besides the ICRC, we met regularly with United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, which also was deeply involved in the humanitarian deliverance of aid, and then there was also the soldiers from the United Nations protective force, UNPROFOR. And I would say last but not least, the European Community Monitoring Mission. We had quite good sources on what was happening, and these sources, particularly the ICRC and the UNHCR, were well represented on the ground. As the Court knows, the International Committee of the Red Cross is mandated by the Geneva Conventions, in this case the IV Geneva Convention to look after the humanitarian needs of civilians in areas of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can I ask you to turn next to an entry in your diary from the 6th of September, 1992. That's P00784, at page 21. And, Ambassador, that's in ICFY book number 1, meeting at 10.00, found on the first page.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, again, looking at the page to the right on the screen, shown on the screen now, there's a -- we see that the meeting's attended by Thierry Germond and Ms. Sadako Ogata, and there's a reference to TG speaking; I presume that's Theirry Germond. And can you read the fourth entry down?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theirry Germond, who was the senior ICRC delegate for all of Europe and had been given the task of monitoring and providing humanitarian aid in Bosnia, said that -- I quote: "Sommaruga was frank in London and none of the Yugoslav parties objected. The Serb quantity is more, but all behave equally badly in quality." Sommaruga, Cornelio Sommaruga, the man he is referring to, was then the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and had spoken at the London Conference at the last week of August 1992. This was unusual, actually, and in his remarks Dr. Sommaruga noted that because the International Committee of the Red Cross normally works confidentially with governments as an impartial, neutral actor, it is, in the ICRC view, important that they maintain this confidential relationship in order to be able to have access to prisoners, civilian and military. But Dr. Sommaruga felt the situation was so horrific in Bosnia that he spoke and gave a major address at the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, at this time I would like to make a motion to exclude any information from the International Red Cross, to strike the answers that have been given, and to preclude further information from the Red Cross. As you know, there's an absolute privilege by the Red Cross from giving evidence in proceedings such as this and also in co-operating by furnishing documents to a party to these proceedings. So we are in a position when the Red Cross evidence is elicited in this trial of not being able to have access to any of the information from the Red Cross by which we could check or verify or even do any further investigation of this. So since a Red Cross official would not be testifying here directly to these matters, I don't think it's proper for there to be indirect testimony which directly quotes what Red Cross persons had said. So on that basis, I would ask that you exclude evidence as to -- coming from the Red Cross. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a specious objection on a number of levels, but let me simplify it and say that I'm about to turn to a public address by Mr. Sommaruga. Clearly to the extent any privileged issue is entailed here, and there's no need to get into it in any more detail, it's waived when a public address is given. So I don't think we need to go any farther than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with the observation of Mr. Tieger. It's a public statement, and the witness can deal with it as such. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, but my motion did actually also include the private statements that were being made as reflected in the diary. So there are -- he's about to go to public statements, but we've also now had testimony about private statements being made by Red Cross officials to Mr. Okun and Cyrus Vance and the others. So I would ask that you address that issue as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The weight of Mr. Ambassador Okun is for the Chamber to assess at a later stage, so as such I don't see any problem in moving along. So motion is denied. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn now, as I was earlier requesting, to P00807. And, Ambassador, as indicated, this is an address by Dr. Cornelio Sommaruga, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross at the London Conference as delivered on 26th of August. And I'd like to turn to some of the things that Mr. Sommaruga said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see at the top of the page to the left, Ambassador, that

utterances.speaker: DR. SOMMARUGA SAID
utterances.text: "The International Committee of the Red Cross has rarely been so outspoken while active in a country affected by conflict." Is that a reflection of what you were mentioning a moment ago about the unusual nature of Dr. Sommaruga's remarks?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He goes on to say that: "All these appeals were made necessary by the seriousness of the humanitarian situation in former Yugoslavia, particularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then toward the bottom of the page he states: "Let me give you the sad picture. "The civilian population is systematically harassed; thousands of civilians are arrested in their homes, brutalised, or even killed. Whole minority groups comprising tens of thousands of civilians are systematically transferred by force or as is currently the case in Sanski Most driven without any protection towards and across the front lines. Hundreds of thousands of civilians have been besieged for several months in cities such as Bihac, Bosanski Brod, Derventa, Gorazde, and Sarajevo. Detainees, the majority of whom are civilians, are held in conditions of extreme hardship in places of detention which are totally inadequate for the purpose. They are ill-treated and hundreds of them have been executed either in places to which the ICRC has been denied access or in places it has been allowed to visit only after --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait just so that we can follow. Can we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And continuing in the first full paragraph at the top left regarding the detainees, most of whom are civilians: "... they are ill-treated and hundreds of them have been executed either in places to which the ICRC has been denied access or in places to which -- in places it has been allowed to visit only after the executions had stopped." And he goes on to talk about the refusal of access to the detention camps in Manjaca and Trnopolje and entry after many demarches at local and the highest political level. Mr. Ambassador, is this the type of information that you, Secretary Vance, Lord Owen, and the others involved in the negotiations were receiving?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was given to us perhaps more directly, but this is a very accurate commentary on what we received. Yes, this is the kind of stuff we got.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the reference in your journal for September 6th says that none of the parties objected to Dr. Sommaruga's observations, his statement. And you've explained that you met with many of the parties, their leadership, and many of the leaders in the area, including Slobodan Milosevic, Dobrica Cosic, Mate Boban, other internationals. Did anyone tell you that the ICRC and others who were reporting what was happening had it wrong, that -- that the ethnic cleansing, the detention of civilians in camps, was not happening?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody denied that. Dr. Karadzic did mention once, I recall, that the Trnopolje camp, which was a particularly bad detention centre run by Bosnian Serbs, holding Bosnian Muslims and Croats, Dr. Karadzic did mention to me once that that camp was open, that anybody was free to leave it whenever he wanted or she wanted. But I have no evidence that that statement is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about the comments by Dr. Karadzic to you and the other negotiators concerning camps and cleansing, but first I want to turn to some of the other leadership figures with whom you dealt during the negotiations. Did other leadership figures within the region acknowledge that ethnic cleansing was taking place?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say they all did. Indeed, on more than one occasion, President Cosic, who was the president then of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and President Tudjman referred to ethnic cleansing by name as ethnic cleansing in a formal note that was issued together, a diplomatic document, and that was not the only time it was referred to. In fact, in all of the conversations about ethnic cleansing with the Bosnian Serb leadership, it was highly unusual, almost never the case, that they denied it. When they were asked about it, the almost invariable response was, "Look what they're doing to our people," or from Dr. Karadzic, "Sarajevo is a concentration camp where our people are being held prisoner, hostage." So that was the typical dialogue about ethnic cleansing. No denial on the part of the accused and others, but, rather, a finger pointing at the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me ask you to look quickly at a couple of references in the journals. First if we could turn to P00784, at page 53. And that would be in ICFY book number 1, a meeting at 9.10, page 2 of the meeting. And in this case I want to look at a couple of comments by President Cosic, to whom you referred. Sorry, that would be a meeting of the 11th of September, 1992. It should be on page 53 of 784. And at the top page at the left, Ambassador, this appears to be a discussion about camps with Cosic saying he'd like to invite Elie Wiesel and similar others to visit camps and see the situation. "Need to clean up." And then if you could continue.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, President Cosic continued by saying to us: "You are justified in asking us to pressure Karadzic, but you should also pressure the Croats and the Muslims to cease offensive." He meant their offensive actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, similarly, if I could ask you to turn next to P00785. That's ICFY book number 1, a meeting at 11.15, on the first page, and electronically that should be found at page 68 of 785.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ambassador. That's the 28th of September, 1992. And if you go to page 68. The date is September 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If page 68 is the wrong page electronically, then we need to go to -- we need to move forward to the 28th. Yeah, that's it. And it should be the ... This may have been copied in a strange way. Can we turn to the very next page, page 73, e-court page 73. Let's see how that is. Okay. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry about the technical problems, Ambassador. I imagine you've been on that page for a while. If I could ask you to look at the entry that follows just after the beginning of that meeting. We see in that first paragraph President Cosic speaking. And if you can -- it begins -- you've got some of the participants in the meeting listed immediately to the right, immediately below where it says President Dobrica Cosic in the box, and then in other box it says regarding BH, and then look down and then there's a reference to ethnic cleansing by President Cosic. Approximately four lines down it seems to say: "Ethnic cleansing continues - all do it."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said, and that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- all right. Now, you have mentioned President Cosic is among those acknowledging the ethnic cleansing that was taking place, and you also mentioned earlier that you brought the matter of ethnic cleansing, the matter of the camps, the detention of civilians, to the attention of Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders and that their response was tu quoque, "The others are doing it too." You made reference to some of the meetings at which such comments were made in your Krajisnik testimony. If I could turn you to at least one other, and that would be the meeting of the 29th of January, 1993. That's ICFY book number 7, a 4.00 meeting, and that would be -- that would be P00789, at page 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the exhibit number again? It's ICFY book number what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's -- for the Ambassador's benefit, he will find it in book number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's P00789, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not 790. What is the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was 06539.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. My list says its ICFY number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the meeting -- you may be right, Your Honour. Your Honour, thank you. It is 790. That is correct. But I believe the page number should be correct. And we'll have to scroll back. It's a meeting of the 29th. And that would be page 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, if I could ask you to look toward the bottom of the page at the beginning of the meeting. That's a meeting with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Buha. And there we see, according to your entry: "Karadzic criticises DLO statements regarding Serbs, especially," and it looks like "Tribune de Geneve interview." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could continue?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lord Owen responded by saying this talk of referendums is impossible. He's referring to the fact that on numerous occasions the Bosnian Serbs offered to hold referenda in the conquered areas, in the areas that they were occupying, and since they had been ethnically cleansed, one understood why they wanted to hold these referenda, and Lord Owen is saying that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then does Dr. -- does Dr. Karadzic continue to --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- raise the issue of what was said in the article and respond to it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic said to Lord Owen: "You said we burn down villages. Many more Serb villages are burned down than Croat or Muslim, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera." The three "et ceteras" mean that this was a common argument that we had heard many, many times before and therefore there was no need to repeat it in the diary. And you can see that Mr. Vance was a little impatient, because the next entry reads: "Secretary Vance: Appeals to get on with the job." To which Mr. Buha responded at length and with some force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And was -- with regard to the comments by Dr. Karadzic in response to the statement about the activities of Serbian forces and burning down villages another of the tu quoque responses to which you referred earlier?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, did Dr. Karadzic ever tell you who was in charge of the forces of the Bosnian Serbs that were the subject of these complaints?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Geneva we had one of such conversations in which Dr. Karadzic said that he was in control of the Bosnian Serb armed forces. They were under his command. And he also said that General Mladic had been difficult to deal with at the beginning, adding that, "You know how soldiers are." And he then indicated that Dr. -- that General Mladic was under his control also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to the meeting of September 17th, 1992. That's P00785, page 25, and that's found in ICFY book number 2, Mr. Ambassador, a 9.00 or 9.10 meeting, and at pages 4 to 5 of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking toward the bottom of the page towards the left, it appears that CRV or Secretary Vance asks first: "What of your irregulars, control." And can you indicate what Dr. Karadzic responded to --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, Secretary Vance asked who controls the irregulars. Dr. Karadzic answered that 5 per cent were not under control. As for the rest, "I control." And then I quote him as saying, and this is the quote: "We can do anything. The army has a unified command. I have full power."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me also ask you to turn to an entry from the 31st of October, 1992. That's -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's P787, and it's page 39. And indicates that at 12.55 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We were on the correct page just a moment ago. That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At 12.55 there's a telecon from Radovan Karadzic from Prijedor for CRV or Cyrus Vance, see memcon. And in that connection, if I could ask you to turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Or ask the Registrar to call up P00811.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, is that the note for the file concerning that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is it, with my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us quickly what that was about? Well, let me assist by simply noting that some of this -- these portions -- the first part indicates the telephone call itself and the time, and Mr. Vance's absence, and it indicates that you raised with Dr. Karadzic the issues of civilians fleeing from Jajce in the direction of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said we were receiving reports that these people were being shelled and that their condition was extremely serious. I'm reading: "Dr. Karadzic said that there had been little or know shelling of Jajce. The town had been captured by infantry alone. He further said that civilians were protected at Jajce and that the town had been taken by a disciplined group of soldiers 'who were not irresponsible.' He said this was a disinformation campaign directed against the Bosnian Serbs. I replied that we had very different information, that I believed it to be reliable, and that in any case he should immediately call his commander on the spot and order him to protect all innocent civilians no matter what. I reiterated that the reports we were receiving said that thousands of people were fleeing Jajce. Dr. Karadzic said this was not so but that residents of Jajce had left earlier. I reiterated in the strongest possible terms that he should call his local commander and order him to cease and desist from any activity directed at innocent civilians. I said this was a matter of the most extreme urgency. Dr. Karadzic said he would call his commander and so instruct him."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was that a further reflection, Mr. Ambassador, of your understanding that Dr. Karadzic was the man in control of the military forces and his affirmation of that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I might mention on the facts of the situation. On that same date in Geneva, October 31st, 1992, I had spoken to Dr. Karadzic at 12.55 p.m. That evening at 10.00 p.m. I was still in my office. If you notice on that page it says "telecon," which means telephone conversation, from Arnie Kanter in the department re: Jajce. And Kanter was the number 3 person in the US Department of State and here he was calling me at 10.00 p.m. on Saturday night. I think that indicates the seriousness of the situation and that our information about the mistreatment of the civilians was accurate. In any case, Dr. Karadzic undertook -- said he would undertake to call his commander and order him to presumably stop doing what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, in an earlier reference in the diary you noted Dr. Karadzic's reference to the unified command of the army and full power and also to his control of 95 per cent of the irregulars. And I want to ask you about a couple of references in the diaries to paramilitaries or paramilitary figures. The first one is found at April 15th, 1992, meeting. That's P00780, beginning at page 22. And, Ambassador, that's in the Vance mission book number 7, a meeting at 6.45 -- that began at 6.45, with Slobodan Milosevic. And if we can look at the entry on the right side of the screen, page -- pages marked 41 in the journal, it appears that Secretary Vance is asking a question about the presence of Arkan. And can you indicate what Secretary Vance inquired and what Mr. Milosevic's response was and how that conversation continued?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan was the leader of a particularly vicious paramilitary group that had been active during the war in Croatia, and then when the cease-fire went into effect, the hostilities ended in 1992, transferred his activities to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this was early days still, April, so Mr. Secretary Vance asked Milosevic: "What about Arkan on the Drina?" Meaning that he had heard that Arkan's forces were active along the western bank of the Drina, particularly in Bijeljina. And Vance added that General Adzic, who was the Commander-In-Chief at that point of Yugoslav Army, says: "He's there." And Milosevic answers: "No. Maybe somebody could be somewhere." That, I should say, was a typical Milosevic answer. Maybe somebody could be somewhere. He later confirmed that: "Arkan was there, but he went on at this point to say it's completely prohibited to go out of Serbia. Arkan was on TV 'advertising himself.'" He was initially 'privately' in Bijeljina, and that answer was so obviously mendacious that Secretary Vance said: "No, that won't wash." And then Milosevic admitted that Arkan was there but said: "Only at the beginning. Rest of the time, Arkan was in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, if I could ask you to turn, quickly, to page 44, and that's page 24 electronically.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Secretary Vance comes back to the subject stating: "Everyone knows Arkan was there." He meant Bijeljina. And then Milosevic answered the tu quoque answer: "Yes, but others are in Bosnia and Herzegovina too."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, let me ask you to turn next to a meeting the following day, this time with Dr. Karadzic. That's the same exhibit, 0 -- P00780, at page 38, and, Ambassador, that's a meeting that began at 12.05, and the relevant entry is found at page 6 of the meeting. I believe that's marked as page 73 in your book. And the following day did Secretary Vance raise the issue of Arkan with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Shall I read the entry from the journal?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary Vance asked Dr. Karadzic and Koljevic: "What about Arkan and other Serb irregulars?" And they answered in tandem: "We have never ever even seen Arkan. In Bijeljina, a Serb caused a -- a Serb caused a problem in a cafe. Then a manipulation occurred and a fight. Then somebody invited Arkan in. Muslims even sent a cable thanking Arkan."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. And I wanted to ask you, the other -- the other day in court, not during your testimony, but this Chamber heard a colloquy between the accused and a witness who was here in which there was repeated references to who had men and who had weapons. So I wanted to ask you whether Dr. Karadzic told you which side had the men and which side had the weapons.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a point he made more than once. I would not say he made it repeatedly or all the time, but he did make that point. And he said that the other side, that is, namely, the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, have the men, and, "We have the weapons. If we give up our weapons, then we are doomed." And what he was referring to in general was the issue of the heavy Serb artillery shelling Sarajevo and other populated places, and the shelling of Sarajevo, in particular, drew the world's attention and was, needless to say, heavily criticised and led to the heavy criticism of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, during the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, you testified that Dr. Karadzic told you before the conflict began that unless the Bosnian Serbs got what they wanted they would attempt to get it through force. That's at page 4173. Did -- and also at -- yeah, basically at 4172 to 4173. Did Dr. Karadzic tell you after the conflict began that the Bosnian Serb use of force would stop when the Bosnian Serbs got what they wanted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but he rarely used the phrase "got what we wanted." He would more often say "We are ready to stop fighting." Of course, at that point, the Bosnian Serb army was occupying 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they in fact had what they wanted, well, almost all of it, so that it was easy to offer stopping the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to a meeting of the 16th of April, 1992. That's P00780, at page 37, and for your benefit, Ambassador, that's Vance mission book number 7, a meeting at 12.05, at a page that's marked 71. And if you could look at the middle of the page, there's a comment by Dr. Karadzic: "We won't fight after map is decided." Can you tell us what that discussion is about and what Dr. Karadzic was indicating to you and Secretary Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina had several components. The ethnic cleansing was one. The question of what kind of state Bosnia-Herzegovina would be was important. I should mention here parenthetically that the 16th of April, 1992, was exactly ten days after Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by the European Community. The next day, the United States recognised it, and it was admitted to the United Nations, so that on the date of this conversation, namely April 16th, 1992, we were talking about a member state of the United Nations. Well, one of the other factors that was always discussed in addition to the nature of the state and the relationship between the ethnicities was the map, who would occupy what parts of Bosnia. And that's what Dr. Karadzic was stating: That when we can agree on who is somewhere, that is to say, a map, then "We would stop fighting."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, did Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders take positions during the negotiations that depended upon the change in the demographic structure or the demographic conditions that had been produced by the ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was involved in the calls for referendums in the areas that the Bosnian Serbs claim for the putative Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of your Krajisnik testimony you made reference to meetings at which there was a call to "accommodate ethnic realities," which you explained was a "very clear, not so subtle reference to the ethnic cleansing." And you referred to a meeting also of September 19th, 1992, where Dr. Karadzic said "We should stop and stay where they are and where we are." Let me also turn your attention, if I may, to a couple of additional references. The first one of -- at the meeting of the 30th of January, 1993, at page 40 electronically. That would be ICFY book number 7, a meeting that began at 10.55.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think that's 790. I believe I indicated 789. My apologies. Thank you. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a Plenary Session, Ambassador, and Dr. Karadzic is indicated speaking in an entry found on the right side of the page. Can you indicate to the Court what Dr. Karadzic was explaining and what Lord Owen's reaction to that was.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an important meeting following the introduction, the formal introduction, of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan - that occurred on January 2nd, 1993, and this was three, four weeks later - because the plan had had a mixed reaction from the three parties, the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Serbs. I have to take a moment to outline the plan for you, because otherwise this entry will be meaningless. So if you would permit me to outline it, I shall, as briefly as I can. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan consisted of three independent parts: First, constitutional arrangements for the state; second, the military arrangements; third, a map of the provincial structure. The parts had to be signed separately, so nine signatures were required, three parties, three parts, and the situation as of January 30th, the date of this meeting, was that Mate Boban and the Bosnian Croats had signed all three parts. They had fully signed on to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. The Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Serbs did not sign, except that the Muslims accepted the military principles. You see at the bottom of this page Izetbegovic: "Accept military principles, but do not accept map and do not accept military" -- excuse me, "accept 9 principles." I beg your pardon. He's saying he accepts the constitutional principles, does not accept the military or the map. And Dr. Karadzic's side had rejected all three. So we had four signatures out of nine that were required, and the purpose of this meeting was to work with the parties and encourage them to sign on to the other parts of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. And Dr. Karadzic, on the very next page, the point you asked about, Counsel, says: "Have already accepted nine principles and most of the map. 'Some details should be a matter of democratic decision.'" "Democratic decision" is in quotes. "If the people could decide democratically, we'd accept." This was the argument for a referendum in the Serb-held areas. Lord Owen responded, as you see from the journal: "I take that as a rejection, which it indeed was." He added: "Too much of the population has been displaced."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, may I just quickly ask you to turn to another entry with reference to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I would propose to take a break now. I'm noting that all the LiveNote have failed, so I hope that technical difficulties could be solved during the break. So we'll take a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the technical difficulties have been solved. I'll try. Mr. Ambassador, I have a couple of administrative matters to deal with before we continue with your evidence, so could you bear with us just for a minute. So, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Robinson, the Chamber has been carefully considering Mr. Robinson's request for a Defence intern to be present in the courtroom during the cross-examination of Ambassador Okun and indeed for each future witness brought by the Prosecution. The Chamber is aware of the practice in some other Chambers and at the ICTR where both the Prosecution and Defence are permitted to bring interns into the courtroom on occasions. However, we view the situation here as rather different in light of the fact that Mr. Karadzic is self-represented. As you are aware, the Chamber gave some considerations in formulating its order on the procedure for the conduct of the trial to how much assistance you, Mr. Karadzic, would need during the course of the proceedings and determined that Mr. Robinson would be entitled to be present to assist you on legal matters, and Mr. Sladojevic or one of your Case Managers would be entitled to be present to assist you on other matters such as the provision of documents, page references, and so on. We are of the view that should you consider it necessary to have additional assistance, you should make such a request in writing, explaining why you believe that Mr. Sladojevic or your Case Manager do not suffice in this particular instance. So we will therefore deny that -- Mr. Robinson's request at this stage, and ask you, Mr. Karadzic, to make any further application in this regard that you wish in writing bearing in mind the Chamber's order on the procedure for the conduct of the trial. And the next thing is regarding the starting of the cross-examination by you, Mr. Karadzic. Given that the evidence of Ambassador Okun covers a lot of fields such that you anticipated length of time for cross-examination amounts to 14 hours, so the existence of that document in question which was the subject of later -- late disclosure in the opinion of the Chamber does not prevent you from being able to start your cross-examination. I gather the examination-in-chief will be concluded during the course of this session. So therefore, on that basis, the Chamber is recommending you to start your cross-examination immediately following the conclusion of examination-in-chief. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, just before the recess, I had asked you about whether Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership took positions that depended upon the change in demographics brought by the ethnic cleansing and you indicated, in the last reference we looked at, the insistence on referendums. I'd also, in that connection, like to turn next to a meeting of the 15th of January, 1993. That's P00789, at page 58, and, Ambassador, that's found in ICFY book 7, I believe -- six, I'm sorry. At a meeting that begins on 11.55 with Mr. Buha, Mr. Lukic, and Mrs. Plavsic. And the particular reference is found at the -- I think the bottom page 5 of that meeting. In any event, it's also depicted on screen at the moment. I wanted to -- if you found the reference, I want you to turn your attention to the remarks of Mr. Buha that can be found at the last entry on the page to the right on screen at the moment. First let me -- let me turn your attention first to -- perhaps it's easier to look at the preceding page, the reference in the middle, the "Corridor," and then below. Do you see that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So we see: "Corridor. We need it." And then: "Perhaps hold referendum to decide." And then the last entry on the page to the right: "Per Kara," I presume that's Karadzic, "identify controversial areas and solve on basis of referendum." And, Ambassador, is that another instance of insistence by the Bosnian Serb leadership on holding referendums in the areas where the demographics had been changed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would object that. I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So on what point do you object?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the distinguished Mr. Tieger is forcing the Ambassador to draw conclusions that are not based on the text. Therefore, my work will be a lot more difficult. Quite simply, I will need a lot more time. Quite simply, I do not agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that most of the evidence of Ambassador Okun was given pursuant to the regime of 92 ter, we allowed some sort of the leading questions so far. So if you could reformulate your question, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, what is Mr. Buha referring to here in that last entry?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the previous page after he says, "We need the corridor," he says: "Perhaps hold a referendum to decide." And then a few minutes later says that: "Self-determination is vital." And I took that to understand at the time, and I'm sure it was correct, actually, that the phrase "Self-determination is vital" is another way of asking for a referendum. And that was my understanding then, and it is now. And he continues to say that Dr. Karadzic has said, this is the last entry on the page: "Per Kara," Dr. Karadzic has said, "identify the controversial areas and solve on basis of referendum." Now, the controversial areas were the areas that the Bosnian Serbs had conquered, and that was the issue with the map, and again this is a call to take a referendum in the ethnically cleansed areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm going to ask you -- you testified about Dr. Karadzic's response when ethnic cleansing by Bosnian Serb forces was brought to his attention, and you talked, in particular, about tu quoque. I'm going to ask you and the Chamber to look next at a videotaped interview, that's P00809. And I would ask that we play several clips from the interview. The first would be clip 6 followed by 7 and 8, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Karadzic: I would like to stress that beside ethnic refugees, we do have ethnic hostages, and believe me, it's much better to be ethnic refugee than to be ethnic hostage. Ethnic hostages are people who are forbidden to leave certain area. This is violation of Geneva Convention, and we strongly demand that civilians in Bosnia and Herzegovina be allowed to move, to leave certain areas. Sarajevo, city of Sarajevo, is the biggest concentration camps for Serbs. From 60 to 70.000 Serbs are imprisoned in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Karadzic: This is homemade. This is Muslim weapon for killing Serbs. They kill them by that, and they -- as a hammer -- taking -- using it as hammer, and they put the eyes out of -- by this part. That's how -- do you know why they do that? They do that to scare the others, to make them to run out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the main plan was Bosnia and Herzegovina to be state without a single Serb, without a single Serb. That is continuation of policy run by fascistic Croatia during Second World War where Pavelic ideology was -- or theory of three-thirds: One-third of Serbs to be extradited to Serbia, another to be converted into Catholic religion, and third one to be killed. So all of them conceived their own states without a single Serb, and that's why they do massacres to scare people from -- into next area, into next village, to make them run. So it's not just without any purpose. It has a purpose."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Koljevic: Well, ladies and gentlemen, I would like to add just a few words about the most serious blame of Serbs with so-called ethnic cleansing. All of you, as media people, know how serious that charge is, and most of you, I hope, know that there was Muslim ethnic cleansing of Serbs. Especially recently in Gorazde and 26 villages which you may visit sooner or later, if you're lucky, from Gorazde along Drina to Bratunac. There are some other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina where there was very serious ethnic cleansing and we have documents and we have names."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, I'm not sure I mentioned that this was a press conference conducted on the 18th of September, 1992, at the International Conference of the former Yugoslavia. I wanted to ask you if the statements of Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic were consistent with what you were hearing from them in response to allegations of the ethnic cleansing that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were entirely consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to -- ask to play one more clip and -- from that press conference, and that would be clip number 2 -- 12, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Reporter: You say that the Serbs have only 35 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the same time, you claim about 60 to 70 per cent of the whole republic for the Serbs. "Karadzic: We do not claim. We own it, and we possess it, and we control it. That's because we have been majority before Second World War, before genocide. During Second World War, the same coalition have killed more than 700.000 Serbs. That's why we are now 35 per cent of population. Everything in terms of ownership is still 64 per cent."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, later in that same press conference, at the page which is marked 0092-9867, a reporter asks again: "You just said that you want three states in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you control the 65 per cent of the Bosnian territory right now." And Dr. Karadzic says: "No, Serbian territory. This is territory which belongs to Serbs." Ambassador, I wanted to ask you if that's consistent with the position taken by Dr. Karadzic with respect to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to which he asserted Serbs were entitled and controlled.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's consistent. And we also heard that argument from President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could call up the transcript of the press conference on screen. I think that's P00809. And that's the page marked 0092-9863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a separate exhibit number for the transcript, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's under the same number, Your Honour, the video and the transcript together. If the Court wishes, we can make provision for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be sorted out. My e-court has only one page. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that it has a separate attachment. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, there in the middle of the page Dr. Karadzic says: "As a matter of fact, Serbian side as well as Croatian side have its own objective, and it's much easier to deal with Croats, because we know they have objective. Muslim side has no objective -- or, rather, Muslim side has unrealistic objective to have the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina only for them to dominate on Croats and Serbs. We are ready to stop animosity with Croats and to stop any fire and to establish commission for delimitation between delimitation of these two ethnic groups." Now, first of all, Mr. Ambassador, can you explain what is meant by "delimitation" in that context?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's talking there of a border between the Republika Srpska, that is to say, the Bosnian Serb territory, and the community of Herceg-Bosna, namely, the Bosnian Croat territory. There was agreement between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats on a number of points, as I've mentioned in the objectives of the three parties, and here he's referring to giving life to that situation, namely, the geographic border between the two ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did Dr. Karadzic make clear to you and to the other negotiators during the course of negotiations why he found the Bosnian Croat objectives realistic in contrast to the unrealistic Muslim objectives?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He used the word "realistic." He might have chosen another word. "Compatible," perhaps, with Bosnian Serb objectives. They were "compatible" might have been more accurate, or "congruent." But as we know, both the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats wanted to carve out of the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina separate individual political entities, and they had discussed that before the fighting began, while the fighting began. For example, in May 1992, Mate Boban and Dr. Karadzic met at Graz to discuss this and other issues. So Dr. Karadzic's remark here is consistent with their actions and consistent with what we understood at the time to be their actions, namely, to partition one way or another Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can I ask you to turn to a meeting of the 17th of September, 1992. That's P785, page 26, and that's ICFY book number 2, a 9.10 meeting, at page 7. And if you could look at the last sentence on the left side of the page, at the bottom of the page on the left, moving on to the text on the very next page, and if you could tell the Court what that says and what's -- what is being indicated at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this meeting was September 17th, in the third week of the international conference, and that particular meeting was with Dr. Karadzic and Misa Milosevic, and Dr. Karadzic says: "The Muslims are losing because their objectives are unrealistic." The same point he made in his press conference the next day: "Neither the Croats nor the Serbs will allow this." Indicating the parallel goals of the Serbs and the Bosnian Croats that I've already mentioned. And he says: "Izetbegovic is aiming at a rule via the high birth rate." We've discussed that earlier. Then he continues: "How to end the war?" And his answer is: "Get the Serbs and the Croats together. Help them to exchange territories. Help Croatia," and he means the Bosnian Croats, "help Croatia to get normal territories." And he goes on to illustrate the point very accurately: "If a table had Milosevic, Hadzic, and me on one side," that is, the Serb side, Milosevic, Hadzic, the leader of the Krajina Serbs in Croatia "... and me on one side and Tudjman and Boban on the other side, we could solve the problem." Well, they would solve the problem via partition, because you notice who's missing is the Muslims. So that's a very straightforward answer to the question of who was who and who wanted what.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just quickly, Mr. Ambassador, two related references. If I could ask you to turn to the meeting of November 28th, 1992, P787, at page 6, and it's ICFY book number 5, a meeting that begins at 9.15. And I'd like to turn your attention to page 5 of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's P788. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, this is a meeting with President Tudjman of Croatia and others. And if I could direct your attention to what is depicted in approximately -- well, the beginning and middle part of the screen on the entry -- on the page to the left. Can you indicate who is speaking and what he's conveying there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the subject of boundaries came up with President Tudjman, and Lord Owen asked: "Can they be changed? And President Tudjman, FT, Franjo Tudjman, said: "Not ours." He said that in very strong, definitive terms. And I capitalised the answers, you'll notice. "Croatia is smaller today than when it entered Yugoslavia in 1919 and smaller than in 1939." And here he was referring to the Cvetkovic/Macek Agreement of August 1939, which, on the eve of World War II, partitioned Bosnia and Herzegovina between Serbia and Croatia. That partition never occurred because the very next month Germany invaded Poland, World War II began, and, of course, it was no longer an issue. But it was on his mind. Indeed, everybody connected with Bosnia-Herzegovina knows of that agreement of August 1939, the "Sporazum," as it was called, because it was a major non-event in Bosnian history, but it also was a formal partition of the state. In any case, he says: "It is smaller than it was at the time. There's the rub." And he goes on to say: "I discussed Bosnia-Herzegovina with Milosevic and Izetbegovic before the current war and said there are two possibilities: "(1) either a confederal Bosnia-Herzegovina," by which he meant three states within a state. The world "confederal" is often used -- another expression was a federal state. Another expression was a composite state. Another expression was a cantonised state. But they all meant the same thing. They meant three states within a state, a non-unitary state. So he says: "... there are two possibilities: "... either a confederal Bosnia or (2) divide Bosnia-Herzegovina into three parts, Serb to Serbia, Croat to Croatia, and a Muslim patch," and that's a quote, "patch," "as in medieval times." Dr. Tudjman was a historian, so he thought in very long terms. But he says: "But now, after the war," meaning after the war has begun, "that's academic." But what this indicates is that both the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats as well as the leaders of their mother countries, namely, Croatia and Serbia, openly maintained the position that the best solution would be to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina between Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Ambassador, I want to turn your attention to a meeting with President Kucan on the 26th --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you talk a bit louder, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure, I'm sorry. I wanted to turn your attention to a meeting with Mr. Kucan on the 26th of January, 1993. That's P790 at page 17, and it's ICFY book number 7, a meeting at 10.00. And I direct your attention to pages 4 and 5 of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We just lost the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the entry that begins: "Your plan is very much based on principles ..." But first I'd like to ask you to explain who Mr. Kucan was and then explain what he's conveying during the course of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Kucan was then the president of Slovenia. He had been a leader of the Communist Party, a young leader, before the war, and it was he who, in 1990, led his country, Slovenia, into a vote on independence. And that vote was positive and -- followed by Croatia, and that led -- that happened directly before the fighting. He was a very intelligent man and a pretty keen observer of events in Yugoslavia. Everybody knew that Slovenia, although small, was the most productive and richest part of the country. So he carried some weight in spite of the small size of Slovenia. And here he says to us: "Your plan -- " and here he's referring to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, "Your plan is very much based on principles. The ethnic structure of 1981 on which your plan or Cutileiro's earlier is based is overtaken by event," OBE, overtaken by events, "because of cleansing, et cetera." Meaning the ethnic cleansing. And he continues to say: "It is better to take the existing situation as a basis for the peace." And he continues by elaborating on that point: "You should adopt Tudjman's and Milosevic's idea of, (A), a transitional government followed by, (B), partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina into three ethnic cantons." And he finishes that statement by saying, and I'm quoting: "The existing reality will win over your principles." And, indeed, that was correct, because the Vance-Owen Peace Plan never was accepted, and subsequent peace plans, of which there were four or five, ended in the Dayton framework agreement of 1995 which divided the country in half as between Republika Srpska and a Muslim-Croat alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does Mr. Kucan continue making his point at the top of the next page, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He goes on in the same vein. "I already told you, Mr. Vance, of my conversation, a very long time ago," I left the word "ago" out, "with President Tudjman in which he said the only solution was partition based on large-scale population transfers. The war has accomplished this process. Discussions between Serbs and Croatians are continuing on partition. This will create two new problems with the Muslims. One, drug pedaling and criminality; and two, Muslim terrorism in Europe in order to keep the Bosnian issue alive. "Is a compromise possible ..." this is Kucan asking himself rhetorically: "Is a compromise possible 'between principles and reality' preserving your ethical approach?" And he continues: "The answer could be found only if it were Yugoslavia alone and not an issue for the Eastern Europeans and Russia. Look at Hungary and it's large minority in Slovakia and Romania. The Slovaks are behaving just like Tudjman towards this -- towards Serbs with their own Hungarian minority. Look at Russia and Russian minorities and other republics."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ambassador, was Mr. Kucan's relating of his discussion with President Tudjman his urging of acceptance of the reality effected by ethnic cleansing consistent with or a reflection of the same discussions you were having with the Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat leadership?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note again that LiveNote is experiencing another technical difficulty. So I propose to take another adjournment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to resume, or you wish to take a break right now and continue -- start your cross-examination after the break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever you would like, Your Excellency. Since I haven't been given Monday, I don't mind either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Our ruling was for you to start and do as far as what you can do today. Given the technical difficulties, Ambassador, we are going to take a break again. We'll break for 25 minutes. We'll resume at quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, to be just clear, we never meant to limit your cross-examination at all. I didn't mean to say to you to conclude your cross during today, far from it. The Chamber is not minded to limit your cross-examination as long as you stick to relevant questions. So with that, let's start your cross-examination. But can I request to you to try to conclude your evidence by the end of next week, given various logistical problems. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I'll do my best to do that, although the examination in chief raised many more topics than we had expected, and therefore the Defence will have many more documents to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to thank you first and foremost for coming with the will to help us to put together the truth about the Balkan crisis and to especially thank you for placing at our disposal your valuable diaries and bringing them with you, your note-books. And I must agree that I will be able to agree with them far more readily than with some of your explanations and thoughts -- or, rather, the explanations and thoughts that Mr. Tieger, through his leading questions, managed to elicit from you. And I did not wish to interrupt him in his examination in chief. Now, do you agree that it will be more important for the Defence, and that it is indeed more important for the Defence what you saw and recorded at -- contemporaneously than what you thought and concluded later on?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Now, may I ask you a question now. How long did you spend preparing for this testimony and the testimony in the Krajisnik trial -- or, rather, how long did you spend in the proofing sessions with Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a couple of days on each.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I regret all the more so for not agreeing to meet with me, because we could have cut down on the time we shall need in clearing up certain dilemmas, but let's continue. I'd like you to help me now understand the role and the capacity and mandate of an ambassador such as yourself with all the repute that you have and the career you followed. Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An ambassador normally represents his country to another country. That would be a bilateral relationship. Given the fact that in our modern world there are many multilateral organisations, ambassadors also represent their countries at these multilateral organisations such as the United Nations, which is a universal organisation; the Organisation of Islamic Conference; EU, that sort of thing. In all cases, I would say, the ambassador is to represent either his country's position, or if he has some other title in another organisation, he would represent the -- that other organisation. In the current matter at hand, Mr. Vance and I were appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. He is guided by the membership of the UN, and in the cases of maintenance and peace and security by the supreme organ, namely, the United Nations Security Council. So we were responsible to him and through him to the United Nations Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Now, performing that function, did you represent your country to a certain measure as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say no, we did not. That may seem odd to you, but Mr. Vance and I, to the maximum degree possible, sought to carry out the mandate that was given us by the Secretary-General. Of course, we spoke with other Americans the way we spoke with everybody who was interested in the matter, but at no point did we represent purely American interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were the political advisor to the Commander-In-Chief of the NATO forces for the Mediterranean, when you occupied that post, did you represent your country?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I was in a command that was headed by the United States, and I was there as his political advisor in Naples. I had a responsibility also to his staff, which was a NATO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me now, please, during the mandate with Mr. Vance, did you inform your country and report back to your country or just to the United Nations? And during your mandate in the NATO command, did you inform both your country or only the NATO command?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the crisis in the former Yugoslavia, we reported only to the United Nations. When I was political advisor to the NATO Commander-In-Chief in the Mediterranean - that was 1973 to 1975 - he reported, as a matter of course, to Brussels and also to the US Navy, because he was, to use the jargon of the day, twin-hatted. He was a US Navy admiral, and he held a NATO command. I did more advising than reporting, but he reported to both, to the navy on to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to explain why I'm asking you these questions. It's because we have difficulty in accessing certain documents. The response we get from NATO is always that they belong to Member States, and the United Nations did co-operate in part, and we hope that at the recommendation of the Trial Chamber they will co-operate, but I would like to know, and it's important for me to know, where the information went. Now, can you tell me in this case, the conference on Yugoslavia, who did you receive your instructions from?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume you're asking about the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, not Lord Carrington's conference. Yes. Instructions? We didn't receive any instructions, at no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It relates to both conferences. Does that then mean that the ambassadors, the mediators, had a free rein, completely free rein, not only in finding ways and means of solving the crisis, but with respect to the results of the crisis, that they had every creative opportunity to do what they liked and say, "Yes, that will be solution"? Because as I understand it, an ambassador is usually there to implement the policy of his own country, and his creativeness is viewed in tactics and in finding ways and means of arriving at a solution. So in the case of the conference on Yugoslavia, both Carrington's conference and the Vance-Owen conference, did you have that creative freedom with respect to an ultimate solution, or were you duty-bound and responsible to someone?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for Lord Carrington, although having observed his conference on more than one occasion I would say that he was probably given carte blanche by the EC, the European Community, to develop the plans for the former Yugoslavia, which he did, and which were ultimately accepted by five republics and rejected only by one republic, only by Serbia. With regard to the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, Secretary Vance and Lord Owen were plenipotentiaries, so to speak. Again, as I said, they reported to the Secretary-General and to the Security Council, and their reports are a matter of record. They were all public. There were no private reports. And they worked inside a larger group that was a steering committee to the conference, but it met only rarely and had no practical effect on the course of the conference. Their job was to continue the work of the Carrington conference to the degree possible but mainly to focus on the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And to that end, all the negotiations with you, Dr. Karadzic, and with the other parties were directed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are privileged to have you here today, because you are living history, as it were, of the diplomatic relations between the West and the Slav countries. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I played a modest role, but I would agree with that up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Because of your vast experience with Russia, the Soviet Union, and Yugoslavia, is that why the Secretary-General asked you to join Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that was part of the reason. The other reason was that he knew I had done quite a bit of negotiating in my day and I also had worked for Secretary Vance previously, and I'm sure he consulted Secretary Vance before he called on me. And so it was a compatible arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you said yourself, throughout your career you were a negotiator. In relation to that, I would like to ask you something. Can we agree that in true negotiations, sincere negotiations that are carried out bona fide, no one ever knows what the exact outcome of such negotiations are going to be. Is the outcome always uncertain? There is always a scope of solutions that may be reached in the process.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would really depend on the nature of the negotiation. If, for example, two parties come together, two states, to sign an agreement on telecommunications, one can be pretty sure that they'll come away with the agreement. If, on the other hand, one has a large multilateral conference such as the recent one on climate change, we all know that there was great doubt that it would succeed. In advance there was doubt. There was also some confusion as to the processes that would be followed, and the net result was no result whatsoever. So it varies a good deal on the type of issue that's before the conference, before the negotiators. Of course, it's important that all sides negotiate honestly and honourably. That does not always happen, but it's important that it happen. Our task at the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia was, as I've noted, primarily Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a washing brief on the other countries -- parts of Yugoslavia, excuse me; not other countries, other parts of Yugoslavia. We had, for example, five working groups at the international conference. The principal one was on Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was headed by a Finnish diplomat who had been seconded to the United Nations by the name of Martti Ahtisaari. A very good man. He later became president of Finland. There was a Working Group, as I mentioned earlier on, humanitarian affairs headed by Madam Sadako Ogata, the UN -- United Nations High Commission for Refugees. There was a Working Group on national minorities which mostly dealt with Kosovo and Macedonian issues. That was a Working Group on confidence in security building measures largely between Belgrade and Zagreb. And there was a Working Group on military arrangements which dealt mainly with Bosnia but tangentially with Croatia, because, as you know, there was a UN peacekeeping force in Croatia. So that was the procedure that was followed at the international conference, and you were able to see that since you were an active participant in the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I'll go back to the question of negotiations. Now I'd like us to look at something else.
