Can we agree that the basis of the Yugoslav crisis was the misunderstanding between Serbia and Croatia -- or, rather, the conflict between them, because as you said yourself, Slovenia and Macedonia obtained independence easily. Although the problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina was far more drastic in the way in which it was ultimately materialised, the core of the Yugoslav crisis was the Serbian-Croatian conflict. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to discuss the negotiations a bit more. Do we agree that in sincere negotiations there have to be concessions made on both sides unless we are dealing with an ultimatum, a take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum, or one that's more drastic than that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's normal for the sides in a negotiation to express at the outset their extreme demands, and then there are what the diplomats routinely call fall-back positions, and that, depending on negotiation, may lead to a fruitful compromise, but it may not. You will recall that one of the V.I. Lenin's most quoted and favourite expressions was that of the quote "Rotten compromise," and that was Soviet policy for many years. But on the whole, it would be expected that the sides would compromise since it would be expected that each would put forth his desiderata, his extreme position, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is quite an exhaustive answer. Now I would like us to look at the following: From that point of view, does a take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum discredit the party that comes out with that ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take-it-or-leave-it ultimata are very rare in conferences and usually do not mean what they say. I can give you an example, Dr. Karadzic, that you yourself are aware of well. The presentation in the summer of 1944 of the Contact Group map, which was presented to the Bosnian Serb side particularly on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, and you chose not to take it or to leave it, and they negotiated with you on the borders of Republika Srpska. So that one can't really answer that question in the abstract. There are times, at the end of a war, for example, when one country surrenders to the other. But even there, even there, at the very highest level, at the most important instances in world history, there have been changes. For example, President Roosevelt, during World War II, announced at the Casablanca conference in 1943 with a very important statement that Germany and Japan would both have to surrender unconditionally. Unconditional surrender was the condition. Well, Germany did surrender unconditionally, but the Japanese government, in the summer of 1945, was negotiating and laid down a condition after the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. That condition, namely, was that the position of the emperor be maintained, which certainly would not have happened without their insistence on it. And the US changed and agreed; yes, the emperor will stay on the throne. So even at the height of World War II, an unconditional surrender was a conditional surrender. So there are very few take-it-or-leave-it examples that one can find. Indeed, the major criticism of diplomats in every country is that they are too eager to compromise with their opposite numbers. That's a routine criticism. Sorry to give you a long answer, but you're asking very important questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Do you recall that the European Community plan within Lord Carrington's conference in the autumn of 1991 was offered to the republics, Serbia included, on the basis of take it or leave it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but it was also negotiated. It's a very good example of what I just said, that the offer of take it or leave it is usually not -- not, in fact, the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that practically none of the Serbian proposals were built into the take-it-or-leave-it proposal that was on the table in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were added to the proposal after Lord Carrington heard all the parties at the end of October. And more than that, the Commission of Arbitrage, the so-called Badinter Commission, the Commission d'Arbitrage, which was appointed formally by the European Community to adjudicate questions -- the legal questions regarding the possible dissolution of Yugoslavia, did come to the conclusion that Yugoslavia was a state in disillusion. It also -- it also passed on the question of which of the four republics that had asked for independence were -- should be granted independence; and the four, of course, were Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia. And the court decided, that is to say, the commission, the Badinter Commission, decided that two of the four republics were worthy of recognition by the European Community. And those two were Macedonia and Slovenia. And the other two, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, were not deserving of immediate recognition. The reason that they gave in either case was the following: For Bosnia and Herzegovina, they felt that the will of the people had not yet been tested, and therefore they said that there ought to be an expression of the will of the people before the country was recognised by the European Community. In the case of Croatia, they said that the Croatian constitution and government did not grant the Serb minority in Croatian enough minority rights and that until those minority rights were granted to the Serb people in Croatia, Croatia should not be recognised. In both cases, the objections of the Badinter Commission were met and those two countries were recognised eventually. So they were not take-it-or-leave-it proposals. They were vetted by the Arbitration Commission, and action was taken on the basis of the decisions of the Arbitration Commission. They were not take-it-or-leave-it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As for the Badinter Commission, did they come to their conclusion on the basis of the state in which the state of Yugoslavia was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Karadzic, which conclusion are you commenting on, the conclusion on recognition or the conclusion on the -- on the condition of Yugoslavia? I assume it's the latter. Yes. The Badinter Commission, in an important avis, an opinion, said - and this was the fall, early winter of 1991 - that the state of Yugoslavia was in a "processus de dissolution," was undergoing a process of dissolution, and that the Yugoslav claim, basically the Serb claim that the declarations of independence by the four republics that we've mentioned, the Serb claim that this was wholly illegal and could be -- was unjustified, that that claim was not correct because the state was, in fact, dissolving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed we'll have to be going back to that yet again, because the distinguished professor Cassese presented a different opinion. As a professor, that is, not as a judge of this court. And he pointed out that these secessions were unlawful and revolutionary. However, I would like to ask you something else. Since Badinter stated that the unresolved questions of minorities were the reason why Croatia's and Bosnia-Herzegovina's claim was not granted, apart from the fact that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not consider themselves to be a minority but a constituent people, did the situation improve from the moment when Badinter reached his conclusion up until the moment when independence was recognised?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The relevant articles were contained in chapter 2 of the draft treaty that Lord Carrington's conference had prepared and presented to the six parties. The Croatians, subsequent to the Badinter Commission's decision, recognised and put into effect that chapter 2, and that solved the problem. And it also was accepted by the leadership - I should say most of the leadership - of the Serbs in Croatia, with the exception of Babic and Hadzic. So, yes, the answer is they did put into effect the shortfall. They made up the shortfall that the Badinter Commission had pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you confirmed just now that Lord Carrington, in his draft, rectified that. However, do you think that these countries, these republics, members of the Yugoslav Federation, Croatia, Slovenia -- sorry, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, rectified that which bothered the Serbs up until the moment of recognition?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on which republic you were talking about. Slovenia had a minuscule --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slovenia's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall, by the way, Dr. Karadzic, that at an earlier meeting you said to us that Slovenia should be recognised. Do you remember that? In any case, as I say, it varied from republic to republic. Twelve per cent of the population of Croatia was Serb. So that was not a huge number, but it was a significant minority, although the Serbs are constituent people. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, about one-third, a little less than one-third, of the population was Serb, who played an important role historically, we all know that, in Bosnia. The situation varied from state to state. I don't think it's possible to say anything more than that. In Macedonia, for example, there was no problem, no fighting, no dislocations. President Gligorov eased the JNA and the Yugoslav authorities out of Macedonia without any fighting, which was pretty much a surprise to everybody, because most people thought that Macedonia would go the way of Bosnia. You recall you told us it would. And that was the majority view, but it did not happen. So the situation was really different in each republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your memory is great. However, do you agree that in the case of Macedonia there was a bit of a difference involved? I said that conflicts were possible not because of the Serbs but because of the large Albanian minority there and that afterwards, indeed, these conflicts did break out. Was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The -- there was no difficulty in the early years as between Serb and Macedonian, but afterwards, yes, there was a problem with the ethnic Albanian minority in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was a short war that ended with the Ohrid Agreement; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was a war or fighting, I wouldn't charge; but, in any case, there was fighting and it was a conflict situation. And it didn't last very long, but there was some fighting at the much later stage - this was the late 1990s - as between Macedonian and the ethnic Albanian minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, your memory was extraordinary, and you recalled my position on Slovenia. Do you remember that I wrote a letter to President Kucan, and this letter was made public as well? In it I asked him the following: To have Slovenia attain its independence through the parliament of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in accordance with the constitution, because that would chart the course for all the rest, rather than resort to a one-sided secession. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, Dr. Karadzic. That would have been probably in early 1991, before I was involved in the Yugoslav matter. But I can believe you wrote that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll try to find that letter. Had Slovenia gone to parliament and become independent lawfully, it would have been easier for us. Do you agree that the Yugoslav authorities, the federal authorities, started building a legislation on the basis of which the republics could attain independence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the constitution of 1974 set forth some general principles as regards self-determination of peoples, "samoopredeljenje," you know it well, I'm sure. The argument, as I recall it in 1991, hinged on the difference or the alleged difference between self-determination of peoples and self-determination of republics. I was never involved in that argument because it was the early years of the conflict with Slovenia and Croatia, June, July, August, 1991, but, of course, I'm aware of the arguments on both sides, namely, the difference between the republics and the Narod, the people. Or the alleged difference, because the parties disagreed on that. All of the Yugoslav parties disagreed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that in 1945, 1943 with AVNOJ, the antifascist organisation, that there were five constituent peoples of Yugoslavia, although six republics were created, and that in that sense there were five fissures and that in the 1960s the Muslim community was recognised as being one of the peoples of Yugoslavia and that the sixth flame was added to the coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the Bosnian Muslims, as we know, were recognised as a nation or a people, as a Narod, in 1974. I believe I'm correct in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Politically I believe that that was in the 1960s, but in constitutional terms I'm sure you're right. Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Now, I'd like to go back a bit and ask you to help us to understand the nature of the negotiations. Do you agree that the negotiating parties observed one another, assessed one another, their determination, their strengths and weaknesses, their readiness to accept and concede or to refuse, and to size each other up, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you put it accurately and well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was it -- is it customary that during negotiations the negotiating parties try and boast and present themselves to be stronger than they in fact are and that they use political speech and atropic [as interpreted] language and linguistics and skills of that kind to make an impression on the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to give a definitive answer on that, but I would say in my own experience that happens very rarely. It does happen, but it happens very rarely, because let us assume that party A to a negotiation goes out and makes a big speech somewhere or goes back to his home country and has a big crowd cheering. That sort of thing does not impress the other side very much. It might even have a negative effect on the other side. So I think that what you described does happen, but it doesn't happen very often. Certainly not in serious negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How would you -- or, rather, would you agree that the party who very early on and very quickly demonstrates a readiness to concede, does it in that way show up its weakness?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that, Dr. Karadzic, because a sincere political negotiation does not depend so much on bravado or expressions of strength. A party that agrees quite early might agree because it's the weaker side; it might agree because it thinks it's getting a better deal from the negotiations than it could otherwise. So there are various reasons that parties concede a position. As I said, it's -- it's common that parties to a negotiation will express their extreme positions at the outset, knowing that they will have a fallback position at some time, and that's what the negotiation is all about. So I think that's more the case than that parties comes in and concede at the outset. Unless, of course, we're talking about a wartime situation where a defeated party comes to sign a surrender agreement. In that case, there's not much negotiation, although even there there's negotiation. After World War I, the First World War, ended on November 11th, 1918, with what was called an armistice, and the peace treaty, the Treaty of Versailles, was negotiated for six months in 1919 and signed on Vidovdan, June 28th, 1919. So there was a negotiation of six months after the conclusion of hostilities. That goes to show that there are many ways to skin a cat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how would you assess a negotiating side whose proposals had been accepted one day and the next day it raises the price, ups the ante, as sincere or insincere?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Dr. Karadzic, it's hard to give a definitive example, because the proposals of the side might have been informal. They might have been presented by persons who were only partially authorised to make those proposals. It's pretty common for proposals to be accepted and still negotiated afterwards. That's why most negotiations take a long time. It's an arduous process, negotiation. And when the matter is a serious matter, the negotiations are more arduous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you would agree, would you not, that once an agreement -- an agreement has been reached, it should be adhered to the next day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it has been formally signed and acknowledged, I think it probably should be. But there are many cases where parties to a negotiation, where countries have taken back their signatures after they've given them, that it's very common, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Countries like that, do they then shoulder the burden for the responsibilities that ensue, the consequences that ensue?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large they -- they could. Of course, it still would depend on the individual terms of the negotiation. In the hypothetical case that you're giving, one would have to know more specifically what aspect of the agreement party A had signed and then unsigned and then what effect that had on the others. It's a bit hard to answer that in the abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume that negotiating is not a simple matter or not a piece of cake, as the English would put it, and if so, would it be a good idea if the negotiators have a certain amount of education in that respect, that they have been educated and trained in the matter of negotiation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are many facets of negotiation and many qualities that good negotiators should have. Ideally they should know their subject matter. They should be good judges of the parties. They should be, in some cases, impartial. Other cases, they, of course, would be partisan. I think it's rare that most negotiators are actually trained in negotiating. If they're lawyers or judges, they have, of course, legal training and experience, and that's why many Secretaries of State in the United States are lawyers. Mr. Vance was one, and many others. Not all of them. Henry Kissinger was not a lawyer -- is not a lawyer. But legal training gives a very strong advantage, and I think that's why it happens. But whether one can say that every negotiation and every negotiator has been trained for negotiation or should be trained for negotiation, I think that's really an unanswerable point. It's a valid point, but one cannot answer it Yes or No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I meant negotiators on behalf of parties, but I'm very thankful to you. You had in mind mediators, but I accept your answer, and I'd like to fine tune it a little and expand it. You consider that a mediator must be impartial, respect the other parties, and so forth; but would you agree that it would be highly detrimental, very harmful, if one party, rightly or not, considered that a mediator, an intermediary, is not impartial, that he is strongly bias in favour of one side?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly would have a negative effect on negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, if both sides were conscious of that or though that way, would the side that is favourised be encouraged to raise the price and make extreme -- call for extreme conditions and act more freely than the other side, the side against whom a mediator -- where the mediator is perceived as being biased, rightly or wrongly so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be the case. I would not say it would always be case, but it could be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to your enormous experience now in our parts, in our part of the world. According to the information we know of you as a sportsman, you went down our rivers, the Drina, in a kayak, and in all wars and crises these rivers and places proved to be important events -- where important political events took place, and also war events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did paddle. I was, in my younger days, an ardent kayaker and paddled on many rivers in Europe, mostly Germany, but also in France on the Ardeche and on the Black Drina, as we called it, in the Yugoslavia. That was in the 1950s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after that, you took place -- you took part in quelling the Cuban crisis, and then you came to the Yugoslav crisis. Before that, you were a high-ranking political advisor to the Commander-In-Chief of NATO for the Mediterranean with a special duty to monitor Marsal Tito's activities, who, at that time, was 83 years old and it was quite clear that the biological clock was ticking for him. Now, do you agree that these were two very important years in Yugoslav history?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from 1973 to 1975? Yes, I would say they were important years, because the constitution of 1974 was adopted, and with the marshal's increasing age, the entire Yugoslav domestic scene was shifting. Power was going towards the individual republics and away from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you that just before your taking up that position, the crisis in Croatia as the mass pock, the mass movement, secessionist movement, had been completed, which Tito solved by replacing the entire Croatian leadership, and some generals were given prison terms, amongst whom was President Tudjman, Tudjman who later became president?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that, as an outsider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then one year later, President Tito, as was customary with the Communists, rightly or for purposes of symmetry, replaced the leadership of Serbia as well, and the reason given was that they were neo-liberals -- or, rather, liberals. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that specifically, but I'm prepared to believe that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was less of a hullabaloo over that because the conflict in Croatia ripened over a period of several years, but if we take a situation in which you have Croatia and Serbia left without their top leadership, an enormous number of leaders, do you agree that Bosnia, Macedonia, and Slovenia in a way had the advantage because they had their old, experienced, and respected leaders?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that could be the case, although in the case of Bosnia, as we both know, Alija Izetbegovic was also gaoled in the early 1970s, not because of secession or problems with the Communist Party as much as it was because of the Islamic Declaration that he had authored and participated in. But I think as a general matter, the fact that the two principal republics of the Socialist Federated Republic of Yugoslavia, namely Serbia and Croatia, were temporarily out of action, so to speak, at the party level probably did leave the smaller republics with a bit for -- a bit more room for manoeuvre than they might have had otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You probably noted the rise of the Muslim leadership, for example, Dzemal Bijedic, a case in point, who became prime minister, a federal prime minister. Hamdija Pozderac, another case in point, who became the absolute master of Bosnia. And Hamdija Pozderac and Branko Mikulic in Bosnia-Herzegovina held all power in their hands. One was a Muslim, the other in -- was a Croat. And so the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being translated and interpreted as an independent undertaking by Branko and Hamdija.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I -- is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is, Do you remember the rise of the Muslim leadership after that crisis? Dzemal Bijedic who became a federal prime minister and Hamdija Pozderac who was the absolute master of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. Not well, but I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, at that time from 1973 to 1975, did you happen to notice somebody else, one of the other actors in the Yugoslav crisis of the 1990s? Any other name come to mind? For example, me. Did you know about me -- of me?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise in saying I did not know of you at that time. Were you perhaps thinking of Fikret Abdic and his role in Bosnia in 1973, 4, and 5? Because I do recall hearing about Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You're quite right. He was also one of the actors, one of the participants, but more in economic terms and economic clashes. I don't mind you not knowing of me, because after 1968 I was a silent dissident and delved in medicine, but did you know about Izetbegovic, for instance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only his name and that he was either the author or the co-author of the Islamic Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're quite right. The Islamic Declaration was written before your arrival in 1970, but Mr. Izetbegovic was tried and his associates were tried with him in 1983, but we'll come back to that. Thank you for mentioning it and bringing the subject up. But this is what I'd like to ask you now: Are your diaries in existence, what you noticed, records of that time when you were the political advisor to the commander of NATO?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not keep any diaries at that time. I was not negotiating anything, so I had no reason to keep a note-book or a journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's unfortunate, because you are a keen observer and always document things very well. Now, Mr. Ambassador, at the time already, could you feel -- did you feel what was going to happen to Yugoslavia? Did you have a presentiment? Do you know when the seeds of Yugoslavia's downfall were sown, because we saw the fruits of it? But was it the constitution of 1974 when the seeds were sown, would you say? And your opinion would be very valuable. And I'm sure with your great experience you could pinpoint that time when the seeds were sown.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Dr. Karadzic. I'm sure there are as many opinions as there are people on that subject, but my own view was and is that the adoption of the constitution of 1974 basically decentralised but did not democratise Tito's Yugoslavia. It gave a great deal of power to the Communist parties of the republics. In that sense, it decentralised. But the modus operandi was still dictatorial. And I think that was a mistake, to put it mildly, on the part of Marsal Tito. And the other fact that led to the disillusion was that after Marsal Tito's death in May 1980 and with the gradual improvement of Soviet/American relations after Mr. Gorbachev came to power in the 1980s, that Yugoslavia lost somewhat of its favoured position in the West, because, as we all know, after the break between Stalin and Tito in 1948, Yugoslavia assumed a leading position in what came to be called the nonaligned movement. And this led to quite a lot of contact with the West and good relations. And those good relations were not just political; they were also military and economic. If I might give you just one really extreme example but a good one: In 1991 when general -- when Secretary Vance and I first sat down with General Kadijevic, the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army, in October 1991, he told us that he had been trained in the United States at Fort Leavenworth. We did not know that. But he knew very well the US Army. So that gives you an example that the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army, the JNA, had been trained in the United States. And on the economic front, the largest debtor to the World Bank from 1945 to 1990 was not some underdeveloped country that you might name or some developing country, it was Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia, at the -- obviously with the help of the Western powers, was granted enormous loans from the international monetary authorities, which obviously helped the economy and therefore assisted Tito in his rule. So that there were many reasons that Yugoslavia persisted as a powerful independent state from the end of World War II till roughly the mid-1980s, but then a decline set in politically, economically. The country did decline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, that coincides with a lessening of Yugoslavia's importance for the West, and it also falls into the picture of the improved relations between the blocs; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In my introductory statement, I said that Yugoslavia came into being and disappeared in accordance with the interests of some countries from the West. Most often it was the European countries of the West. In 1918, Yugoslavia was created instead of Serbia that was proposed by the London Agreement, so that there would not be a Croatia and a Slovenia. In 1941, Yugoslavia broke up because Germany was stronger. In 1945, Yugoslavia was created because Germany lost the war. In 1991, Yugoslavia disappeared because Germany became stronger. What do you say to that thesis?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. Without rehearsing 80 years of history, touching the highlights, I would say that Yugoslavia was created at the behest of the Yugoslavs. It was not, for example, a product of Versailles, which many people say and think it was. No, that was not the case. The hope that the southern Slav peoples would some day unite goes back to the mid-19th century when it was put forth largely by Croatian journalists, artists, thinkers. But when the republic was formed in 1919, and it was not a republic. The original name, as we know, was the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. The name Yugoslavia was only given to the country by the King in 1929 to avoid emphasising the ethnic - excuse me - to avoid emphasising the ethnic aspect. Germany had nothing to do with that. Obviously Germany had nothing to do with the situation in 1919, since it had just been defeated in the first war, the Great War. In 1945 -- well, 1945 was preceded by the AVNOJ republic, in 1943, declared by Tito in Jajce, incidentally. Jajce was the place where Tito's Yugoslavia was born. And again, this was a -- entirely a Yugoslav operation, to be sure. It depended on the defeat of Germany in World War II, but nobody but Yugoslavs fought in their country, although it has to be admitted they also fought each other. We had the fascist Ustasha and the Partisans and the Serb Chetniks all fighting at the same time, fighting the Germans or fighting each other. So that was a complicated situation. But Tito's rule was pretty consistent until his death in 1980, and we've discussed the situation after that. I really don't see Germany playing the role that you ascribe to it, except that in the fall of 1991, during the Croatian business, Germany took a very strong anti-Yugoslav and pro-Croatian position. For example, it said it would recognise Croatia regardless of what the rest of the European Community did. That is correct. At that time, Germany played an important role, but that was the only time. Based on my experience at the conference on Bosnia and earlier, I saw no particular German role nor any particular German interest in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Croatia was always their baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since then, the popular song Danke Deutschland has been well known in the context of Croatia. Germany did not figure prominently for as long as things moved the way they wanted them to move, but if the USA and other European countries moved in a different direction, then Germany even resorted to blackmailing other members of the European Community. It's Warren Christopher, President Clinton, Henry Kissinger, the presidents of France that speak of this. It is not me saying that. Even some British prominent figures say that. Germany was assessed by them as a generator of the Yugoslav crisis and ultimately the party that caused the catastrophe because they were in favour of the premature recognition of the republics. However, we'll go back to that. Are you familiar with the position -- positions, rather, of these persons that I mentioned in the context of Germany's role?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any detail, but I'm aware of their position and of the German position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to go back to the very interesting thing that you said. Instead of having one dictatorship through the constitution of 1974, we got six dictatorships. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned that President Tito did quite a bit within the framework of Yugoslavia to weaken Serbia and that that was not exactly being carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall that the Macedonian statesman Lazar Kolisevski, after the first crises in Kosovo in 1981, disclosed that it had been a big mistake to pursue a domestic policy based on the motto of a weak Serbia, meaning a strong Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after 1974, tens and hundreds of thousands of Serbs and Croats left Bosnia because of the dictatorship that existed at republican level? Serbs and Croats, especially the intelligentsia, artists, intellectuals, Croats primarily to Zagreb and Croatia and Serbs primarily to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that said, Dr. Karadzic, but I, frankly, wonder whether that's accurate. I recall -- we all know, for example, that in 1984 the Winter Olympics, a major, major international event, were held in Sarajevo, and I can't imagine that happening without the willing consent of almost everybody in Sarajevo, because it's a very big public occasion, an Olympics. So I don't really have any answer to your question, but I rather doubt it in some respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I were to show you statistics or if I were to give you the names of prominent individuals who fled from Bosnia practically, or if I were to tell you that what happened was that the then-authorities of Bosnia arrested 250 Serbs at the same time, for instance, then you would probably have a different view of that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, I would believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you of something that is called "gerrymandering." It was named after Jerry Mander, who resorted to electoral engineering, making it possible for a smaller party to win an election, although that could not have been possible in natural conditions, as it were. Are you aware of the phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm well aware since gerrymandering was an American invention in the 18th century, and it goes on to this day, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I were to tell you, Mr. Ambassador, that the Bosnian Serbs, over the past -- or, rather, over the 20 years before the crisis, underwent an involution in every conceivable way on the basis of gerrymandering municipalities and regions. I could give you a few examples of that. Serb municipalities were abolished in the following way: They would be annexed to a neighbouring Muslim municipality, thereby turning the Serbs into a minority. Another way of gerrymandering was to have a group of Serb municipalities taken out of another group, say Visoko Krajina would be separated from Banja Luka and attached to Bihac, thereby turning the Serbs into a minority. Or, for example, the municipalities of Semberija would be attached to Tuzla thereby turning the Serb municipalities. Modrica, Doboj, Derventa with Serb majorities would be attached to another group so that they would become a minority. Also in the case of Gorazde, Eastern Herzegovina would be attached to Mostar thereby turning the Serbs into a minority. And in these centres there would be an abrupt development, because these centres were the focus of political and economic power. Would you agree to the possibility of this leading to the devastation of the Serbs and their economic and political downfall?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that if that happened, it would only lead to their economic and political downfall if many other steps were taken. There's nothing automatic about political and economic downfall stemming from gerrymandering, which basically concerns the voting procedures of a state. It is why in the United States, to this day, most of the representatives in the US House of Representatives are overwhelmingly re-elected, because their districts have been gerrymanded to suit one or the other parties. But I don't think it leads directly to economic problems or, as you say, downfall, unless there were a whole series of other steps taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's what I meant. It's just being used tentatively, the term "gerrymandering." It went on for decades. Also, overall financial life and any other kind of life takes place in a centre such as Mostar, for instance. Thirdly, the measures that you speak of, you are right, but these measures are quite possible in the absence of democracy, that is to say, while there was a republican dictatorship, the one that we spoke of. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible, surely possible, to disadvantage one or another group against another group, but I think the Bosnian Serbs still commanded a great deal of power and attention as late as 1991. It would take a deep exhaustive academic analysis to determine whether and to what degree the Serbs in Bosnia were disadvantaged in the 1970s and 1980s, and I don't know that that's been done. Perhaps it has, but I really couldn't speak to that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that suggestion. I will put that to this Trial Chamber. However, let us try to agree on matters. After the first democratic elections in which my party won one-third of power, would you agree that the position of president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a position that carried a lot more weight than the position of the speaker of parliament?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the other executive position, that is to say of the prime minister, is much stronger than that of the speaker of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would agree with that. The speaker of the Assembly had a great deal of power. The prime minister suffered, so to speak, because the president of the Presidency had a commanding position. We could see that, for example, even during the Bosnian conflict when the president was Alija Izetbegovic and the prime minister -- a Muslim, Izetbegovic, and the prime minister, Mile Akmadzic, a Bosnian Croat, and Akmadzic did not really carry much power beyond the Croat community. Of course, he was strong there. So I think that the president of the Assembly, for example, the Bosnian Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, had much more power than Akmadzic both in the country and within his own party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you will agree with me in saying that the power of the president of the Assembly -- well, I mean it's the Assembly that has power. There are three institutions, the Presidency, the Assembly, and the Government. The Presidency was a collective organ, although Mr. Izetbegovic often presented himself as Presidency of the republic, but he was not president of the republic; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In fact, he did not receive of most votes, as you know, in the election of 1990. Mr. Abdic received more votes than he did, as the leader of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree. That is correct. Do you agree that that works in the favour of the Bosnian Muslims, because Fikret Abdic was a secular politician and he had a pro-European orientation when we compare him to Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was more secular than Izetbegovic. That is true. And he was very popular in the far west, in the Cazinska Krajina. The Bihac pocket was his home base and preserve, including during the fighting. Unfortunately, as Dr. Karadzic mentioned earlier, his focus was on economic matters, and he had gone to prison for behaviour - I should say misbehaviour - with money, and this affected -- naturally affected his reputation with the other communities and, above all, with the Bosnian Muslim community. I'm referring to the Komerc case. I'm sure you're aware of it. So that his small majority in the election of December 1990 was not enough to automatically make him president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the president of the Presidency, Izetbegovic, was a Muslim; the first prime minister was Jure Pelivan, a Croat; and the speaker of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the minister of the interior was Alija Delimustafic, a Muslim; the minister of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was Jerko Doko, a Croat, and that those are the two ministries of force? There is no third one because the secret services were within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serbs asked for the Ministry of Agriculture and got it, as well as the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Science, and the like, ministries that were quite far away from the ministries of force?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I'm not sure that they had them, but I hear you saying it so I believe it. But in connection with the word "force," it's important to remember that there was something called the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, which had overwhelming power, and by 1991, 1992, was largely, almost exclusively, a Serb army. So I find it difficult to equate the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Yugoslav People's Army as regards force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I meant primarily was the Ministry of Defence. However, will you agree that in Yugoslavia there wasn't anything like the FBI? There wasn't a federal function of this nature. Basically, the situation was one as if it were a confederacy. Basically, the ministries within the republics were sovereign. They only had some formal ties to the federal ministry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not intimately connected with the interstices of Yugoslavia administrative organisation, but I can believe that that would correct, given the strong decentralisation that had happened after the constitution of 1974 took effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I assure you that there was not a single executive police function at the level of the federal state that can be compared to the FBI or the CIA in the United States. However, before we adjourn for the day, I would like to ask you something else. Do you remember that NATO, in 1978, held big manoeuvres, military exercises, on the basis of what would happen to Yugoslavia after Tito's death, and do you accept that they relied on your advice, although you were not there at the time, but they did rely on your knowledge what carrying out those manoeuvres?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're very flattering, Dr. Karadzic. In 1978, I was in Geneva, working on the SALT II Treaty with the Soviet Union. I had absolutely nothing to do with Yugoslavia at that period. That there were manoeuvres because of uncertainty regarding what might happen vis-à-vis the Soviet Union after Tito passed from the scene, I can well believe that that was the case, because there was indeed a concern about the future of Soviet Yugoslav relations. And in this connection it's relevant to bear in mind that in 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan, the first time the Soviet army, the Red Army, had invaded a country that was not a fellow Communist country, because they'd already invaded Poland and they'd invaded Czechoslovakia. But the 1979 invasion of Afghanistan was a major event and led to a serious worsening of East/West relations as you might expect. So there was reason to be concerned about a Soviet reaction to Yugoslavia post Tito.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, these expensive manoeuvres - they probably did cost a great deal - were carried out with a view to the following: All sorts of things could have been expected to happen in Yugoslavia after President Tito's death; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I remember, the overwhelming concern was, What would the Soviet Union do, if anything? I don't remember many, if any, discussions on the domestic side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Ambassador, we have the CIA reports from a later date, in all fairness, forecasting the disintegration of Yugoslavia and a crisis after Tito's death. Indeed, these forecasts were heard all the way up to 1989; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The CIA reports of the 1980s were based on the 1981 census. At the census, it's standard procedure to be asked, What ethnicity do you belong to? Are you a Serb, a Croat, a Muslim, an Albanian, a Jew, whatever? Not just the constituent peoples were counted, but all of the peoples. There were -- there's a fairly substantial Hungarian minority in Serbia. And one of the choices under "Nationality" was Yugoslav. And the 1981 census, less than 10 per cent of the respondents answered "Yugoslav." Something like 7 per cent. So that meant that 93 per cent of the people in the country did not feel any attachment to the nationality called Yugoslav, and that was the basis, as it turned out a correct basis, for the Central Intelligence Agency to point out the internal difficulties that the state might some day face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that, we will adjourn today. Mr. Karadzic, while the background, historical background, may be interesting, we have heard little, except for a few exceptions, that is relevant to the period relating to the charges against you. So I hope you would move on to the period on Monday. We will resume again on Monday, 9.00. I hope everybody has a nice -- good weekend.
